r.label: Question 3

oe.title: Melting points of non-metal elements
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Covalent network elements (carbon as diamond or graphite, silicon, boron): melting breaks strong covalent bonds, so very high melting points.
Covalent molecular elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, P₄, S₈, C₆₀): melting only breaks weak London dispersion forces between molecules, so low melting points.
Larger molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces: S₈ and P₄ are solids, Cl₂ is a gas; I₂ is a solid.
Monatomic noble gases have only weak London forces between atoms, so very low melting points that increase down the group (more electrons).
So the statement is true: structure (network, molecular or monatomic) and bonding (covalent bonds or intermolecular forces broken) determine melting point.
Diagrams to consider
Diagram of a covalent network (diamond) and a molecular element (e.g. P₄ or S₈) showing the forces broken on melting.
Sketch of melting points across period 3 (high for Si, low for P, S, Cl, Ar).
Diagram of temporary dipoles creating London forces.

r.label: Question 9

oe.title: Chemicals in laundry products
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Soaps and detergents: the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail dissolves in grease and the hydrophilic (ionic) head in water. Agitation forms ball-like structures (micelles) that are washed away. Soapless detergents also work in hard water.
Bleaching agents are oxidising agents (e.g. hydrogen peroxide, chlorine-based bleach). They oxidise coloured compounds in stains to colourless ones.
Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins): proteases, lipases and amylases catalyse hydrolysis of proteins, fats and starch into smaller water-soluble molecules.
Enzymes work at lower temperatures (saves energy) but are denatured at high temperature (hydrogen bonds break and shape changes), so wash at the recommended temperature.
Water is a polar solvent for ionic and polar substances; non-polar stains need detergent.

Diagram of a detergent molecule and a micelle around a grease droplet.
Ion-electron equation for an oxidising agent, e.g. H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O.

Sketch of enzyme activity against temperature (optimum, then denaturing).
